newsitem.title: USA: Philippine peso crash to test new IMF funding rule.
newsitem.headline: Philippine peso crash to test new IMF funding rule.

text.p: The Philippines currency crisis is giving the International Monetary Fund its first opportunity to try out emergency financing rules introduced after the Mexico crisis in early 1995.

An IMF source, who asked not to be named, said accelerated procedures to offer the Philippines a support package of at least $600 million relied on rules established under the so-called "Emergency Financing Mechanism" of the IMF.
These rules aim to let the IMF respond more quickly to financial problems around the world, and they only kick in when a crisis is there or is thought to be on the cards.

But the IMF said Thailand, whose own currency crisis triggered that in the Philippines, was not talking about IMF emergency aid at present, although IMF experts were holding talks with the Thai authorities.
"No negotiations on a programme for Thailand have started so far," a spokesperson said.

The two currency crises -- both Thailand and the Philippines reluctantly allowed their currencies to float after massive speculative assault -- have unsettled authorities elsewhere in the region and prompted talk that speculators might turn their guns elsewhere.

The Malaysian central bank has promised tough measures to defend the ringgit, but Indonesia unexpectedly widened the dollar-rupiah trading band on Friday, allowing the central bank extra room to cope with external shocks.
"Malaysia is next in the firing line," said Dimitri Zenghelis, country economist for Malaysia and the Philippines for the Institute of International Finance.
"There is not much the international financial community can do, it's very much market dominated and market inflicted."
But analysts said a support package for Thailand could come from sources other than the IMF.

"Thailand has decided not to operate within the IMF framework," said David Hale, global chief economist for Zurich Kemper Investment Group. "They plan to get $10 or $20 billion from Japan, through private channels, not from the IMF."
Japan may be prepared to help its regional neighbour, but its banks are unlikely to make that much cash available.

The IMF introduced its emergency procedures after a $50 billion international loan package to help Mexico out of a financial crisis that was having a damaging knock-on effect on emerging market economies around the world.
The loans, not all of which were taken up, included $17.8 billion from the IMF, some of which has already been repaid ahead of time.

"Emergency procedures would be expected to be used only in circumstances representing or threatening to give rise to a crisis in a member's external accounts that required an immediate response," the IMF said in its last annual report.
"The potential for spillover or contagion effects would be an important consideration in a decision to activate the emergency financing mechanism."
The Philippines, unlike Mexico at the time of its crisis, was already operating under an IMF-approved economic reform programme.

The IMF said $600 million of the money to go to the Philippines would come from cash that had not been disbursed under the Extended Fund Facility, although "additional financial resources" would also be available when the board met to discuss the situation in the coming days.
